tagline: Shipbuilding towns, a cable ferry and the northern cypress.
intro: From US 13 at Bridgeville Road the byway runs through Seaford, crosses the Nanticoke River on the Woodland Ferry and goes on through Bethel and Laurel to Trap Pond State Park, about 35 miles of farmland, woods and small towns.

These were water towns first, building ships and trading by river, and after the railroad came in 1856 Seaford and Laurel sent oysters, fruit and baskets north. Bethel's yards on Broad Creek turned out the Chesapeake sailing ram, a flat-bottomed three-masted schooner that needed only a small crew.

moments.title: Woodland Ferry
moments.text: A public ferry has crossed the Nanticoke here since at least 1793, and the state runs it year-round as the last cable ferry in Delaware, six vehicles at a time.

moments.title: Old Christ Church
moments.text: The 1772 wooden church near Laurel has never been plumbed or electrified, and its high box pews carry the family names in chalk.

moments.title: Trap Pond State Park
moments.text: Lumbermen dammed the outflow to power a sawmill for the bald cypress, and the pond they made lies in the northernmost park in North America with cypress in it.

sources.label: DelDOT, Delaware Byways: Nanticoke Heritage Byway
